To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the incidence of severe hepatic injury in neonates was 2.3% in a population of 4,000 deliveries; 2) the injury is associated with antenatally, perinatally or post-natally acquired risk factors; 3) the diagnosis of the hepatic lesion is made by ultrasonography; 4) the injury may be complicated by hypoglycemia, coagulation disorders, ascites or pleural effusion
The liver is the most common site of injury in neonatal abdominal trauma.
the use of ultrasound in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) is safe and feasible.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neonatal jaundice is not an indication for routine liver ultrasonography.
neonatal hepatic injuries are usually associated with a combination of antenatal and postnatal factors and are not necessarily associated with a history of birth asphyxia.

the neonate with a history of difficult delivery or antepartum maternal trauma and/or with a history of prolonged or difficult resuscitation and/or a history of fetal distress or a history of a large for gestational age infant should have an ultrasound scan of the liver and gallbladder performed to exclude the diagnosis of neonatal hepatic trauma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of ultrasonography in the neonate with suspected hepatic injury is a useful adjunct to clinical evaluation.

ultrasonography is an important tool for diagnosing neonatal hepatic injuries, and that it can provide information about the extent and location of the injury, and the presence of complications such as biliary leakage.

neonates who present with jaundice should be evaluated for the possibility of a hepatic injury.
